prompt.context: You find out you have a long-lost uncle, and he is a fruit cart vendor at a street corner in downtown Boston. He sells his fruit only on weekdays to morning and evening commuters, as well as downtowners going on lunch breaks. Your uncle realized that you are a business-school student, and he thinks you might be able to make his business more profitable. He wants to increase his profit during this summer by 10%, which would be $1,000 over last year's profits, and he will plow these profits back into the business. In order to do this, your uncle wants to expand into selling vegetables. He is known for having high-quality fruits, which he gets from his buddy who is a wholesaler. He plans to use similar high-quality suppliers for his vegetables. Your uncle operates in a really good location: a well-trafficked spot in the business district near a busy train station.
prompt.question: Can your uncle reach his goal of increasing profits by $1,000 next year by expanding into selling vegetables?

clarifying_info.q: What is the estimated demand for vegetables?
clarifying_info.a: By talking to customers, he has estimated a potential demand of 20 vegetables per day.

clarifying_info.q: What price will he sell vegetables for?
clarifying_info.a: He expects to sell each vegetable for $1.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost per vegetable?
clarifying_info.a: The cost of each vegetable is 75 cents.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any permit or operating cost changes?
clarifying_info.a: The annual cost of his permit to operate is $1,000. These costs will increase by 20%.

clarifying_info.q: Will adding vegetables affect fruit sales?
clarifying_info.a: Cannibalization will decrease fruit sales by 5%.

clarifying_info.q: Will there be any cross-selling benefits?
clarifying_info.a: Cross-selling to certain customers will generate an additional 5% of revenue.

He generally serves three types of customers: morning commuters, evening commuters, and downtowners on lunch breaks. He sees more morning and lunch customers, but evening customers buy for home, so he sells roughly equal proportions of his fruits to each type of customer.

clarifying_info.q: Is there competition from other vegetable vendors?
clarifying_info.a: There are no competing vegetable vendors nearby. Fruit customers generally get their vegetables from supermarkets near home.

clarifying_info.q: What is his expertise with vegetables?
clarifying_info.a: Your uncle has been in the fruit business for 20 years and his customers appreciate his knowledge of peak seasons and quality fruit selection. His knowledge for vegetables is very limited.

framework: Profitability: Revenue (volume x price) and Costs (variable + fixed)
Customers: Similarities/differences to fruit buyers; ability to cross-sell
Competition: Other vendors in the area; where customers currently get vegetables; likelihood of switching
Product: Uncle's expertise with vegetables; which vegetables to offer; spoilage risk
Other considerations: Cannibalization of fruit sales; cross-selling opportunity
Resources: Financing for expansion; cart space

questions.prompt: Calculate the incremental annual profit from selling vegetables.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate per-unit margin, daily profit, and annualize using weekdays only (5 days x 52 weeks).

math.setup: Margin per veggie = $1.00 - $0.75 = $0.25. Daily profit = $0.25 x 20 units. Annualize over 5 days/week, 52 weeks/year.
steps: Annual veggie profit: $5.00 x 5 days/wk x 52 wks/yr = $1,300

questions.prompt: Calculate the additional revenue from cross-selling.
questions.guidance: Cross-selling adds 5% on top of existing fruit revenue. Current annual profit is $10,000, implying fruit revenue is at least that. Apply 5% to the current profit base.

math.setup: Current annual fruit profit = $10,000 (since $1,000 increase is 10%). Cross-selling adds 5% of that.
steps: New fruit profit from cross-selling: 5% x $10,000 = $500

questions.prompt: Calculate the profit lost due to cannibalization of fruit sales.
questions.guidance: Cannibalization reduces fruit sales by 5%. Apply to the current fruit profit base.

The permit cost increases by 20%. The annual permit cost is $1,000, so the increase is $200. Note: the raw case text shows 30% x $1,000 = $300 but labels it 20% increase; the net number used in the total is $200 (20% x $1,000).

questions.prompt: Sum up the total net new profit and compare to the $1,000 target.
questions.guidance: Combine all incremental profit/cost items to determine if the uncle meets his goal.

math.setup: Total new profit = veggie profit + cross-selling gain - cannibalization loss - permit increase.
math.answer: $1,100 net new profit, which exceeds the $1,000 target by $100

brainstorming.prompt: What risks or qualitative factors should the uncle consider before expanding into vegetables?

categories.name: Product expertise
ideas: Uncle has 20 years of fruit knowledge but very limited vegetable knowledge
Lack of expertise may lead to higher spoilage rates eating into profits
Customers may lose trust if vegetable quality is poor

categories.name: Customer fit
ideas: Current customers are commuters and lunch crowd — vegetables for home cooking may not appeal
Need to survey customers on which vegetables they would buy
Cross-selling works best if vegetable needs overlap with current customer habits

categories.name: Competition
ideas: No nearby vegetable vendors is a positive signal
Customers currently buy vegetables at supermarkets near home — habit change required

categories.name: Resources & operations
ideas: Uncle needs at least $200-$300 upfront to finance permit increase and expansion
Cart may not have physical space for vegetables alongside fruit
Vegetable supply chain setup required through wholesaler

categories.name: Margin buffer
ideas: At $1,100 net profit he only exceeds target by $100 — very thin buffer
Any spoilage, lower demand, or cost overrun could eliminate the gain

recommendation: At current estimated demand levels, your uncle would generate $1,100 in incremental profit, just surpassing his $1,000 target by $100.
Expanding into vegetables is financially viable if demand and cost estimates hold.
risks: Lack of vegetable expertise could lead to quality issues, spoilage, and customer relationship damage
The margin of safety is only $100, leaving little room for error
Uncle must secure at least $200-$300 in upfront financing for the permit increase and cart expansion
next_steps: Conduct informal surveys of current customers to gauge vegetable preferences and potentially increase daily demand beyond 20 units
Identify a reliable vegetable wholesaler, ideally through existing fruit supplier network
Plan cart layout to ensure there is physical space for both fruits and vegetables
